analysis.one_liner: Lets companies own unlimited TV and radio stations and exempts media mergers from antitrust review.
analysis.headline: The bill never moved: Senator Rand Paul introduced it with zero cosponsors and the Senate Judiciary Committee took no action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any single company own an unlimited number of radio and TV stations, and would bar the FCC from stopping one company from owning both newspapers and broadcast stations. It would also change antitrust law so that mergers in TV, radio, and newspapers could not be challenged as reducing competition. It offers one thing for struggling news publishers: a four-year shield from antitrust lawsuits so newspapers and news sites could join together to bargain with giants like Google and Facebook over how their stories are used.
analysis.who_benefits: Large broadcast companies and newspaper chains, which could buy up stations and papers without any cap and merge without antitrust challenge. Local and digital news publishers also gain from the bargaining shield against the biggest online platforms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big broadcasters, newspaper chains, news publishers

how_it_helps.text: Removes all FCC limits on how many radio and TV stations one person or company can own, and directs the FCC to repeal its existing ownership rule (47 CFR 73.3555).
Prohibits the FCC from placing any limit on a company owning daily newspapers and full-power broadcast stations at the same time.

Amends the Clayton Act so that market share gained from a TV, radio, or newspaper acquisition cannot be considered to substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly — in practice removing merger challenges in those markets.

Creates a four-year safe harbor letting print and digital news organizations negotiate collectively — or withhold content together — with online distributors that have at least 1 billion monthly active users, without violating federal or state antitrust laws.

analysis.who_pays: Readers and viewers, who would face a media landscape owned by a smaller number of larger companies, with fewer independent local voices in any given market. The biggest online platforms would also face collective bargaining demands from news publishers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Viewers, readers, and large online platforms

drawbacks.text: Removing the FCC's station-ownership caps would allow unlimited consolidation: one company could own any number of radio and TV stations, including cross-owning the local newspaper and local stations, concentrating control of local news and information.
The Clayton Act amendment would strip regulators of the ability to challenge media mergers on competition grounds, no matter how large the combined market share.
The bargaining safe harbor permits news companies to act together in ways that would otherwise be illegal collusion, and overrides state antitrust laws that would penalize that conduct.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes a genuine help for news publishers with a large giveaway to media consolidation. The bargaining safe harbor could give local newspapers real leverage against Google and Facebook, which many local outlets need to survive. But the price is steep: unlimited ownership of broadcast stations, newspaper-broadcast combinations, and a near-total antitrust exemption for media mergers. On balance, the consolidation provisions outweigh the bargaining provision, since fewer owners of local news sources is the very trend that has hollowed out local journalism.

outcome.mechanism: Paul introduced the bill in the Senate with no cosponsors, and the Judiciary Committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the Local News and Broadcast Media Preservation Act on December 17, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No cosponsors signed on — the cosponsor list shows zero members from either party.
The bill's only further action was the initial committee referral; no hearing, markup, floor vote, or House action ever followed before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the FCC's ownership limits and antitrust review of media mergers remain in place — and the largest online platforms avoided facing a legally protected bargaining bloc of news publishers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Platforms kept free news content; ownership limits stayed

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day it was introduced and then took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill, no cosponsors from either party signed on, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill removes every FCC cap on how many radio and TV stations one company can own and lets broadcasters combine with newspapers. Fewer owners means fewer independent local news voices, which has historically meant less local coverage and watchdog reporting.

Cross-ownership of newspapers and broadcast stations would be unregulated, and media mergers could not be challenged under the Clayton Act. The gain to owners comes at the cost of ownership diversity for the communities those outlets serve.

The four-year antitrust safe harbor would let news organizations band together to demand payment and better terms from the biggest online platforms. This is the bill's one provision whose interest runs alongside the public's interest in keeping local journalism alive.

industries.industry: Big online platforms (services with 1B+ monthly users)
industries.note: The safe harbor applies only against distributors with at least a billion monthly users, meaning Google and Facebook alone, which would have faced coordinated demands from news publishers to pay for the content their sites display.
The Clayton Act amendment would bar regulators from treating market concentration in TV, radio, or newspapers as a competition problem, narrowing the government's merger toolkit in those markets.
